title: How do you prepare for an OSHA inspection of training?
description: How OSHA compliance officers test training under the Field Operations Manual, which standards require certifications, and the records to keep ready.
shortAnswer: To prepare for an Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) inspection of training, assume compliance officers will interview employees privately, review your written programs, and ask for the certifications and records that specific standards require. Keep standard by standard training certifications current, make sure training was delivered in a language and vocabulary workers understand, and document how work rules are communicated and enforced, because the Field Operations Manual ties training to employer knowledge and to the employee misconduct defense.
keyTakeaways: OSHA's Field Operations Manual (FOM) tells compliance officers to review programs such as hazard communication, lockout/tagout, emergency evacuation, and personal protective equipment, and to interview non-managerial employees in private.
Failure to train and supervise employees about a hazard is listed in the FOM as evidence that the employer could have known of a hazardous condition.
To use the unpreventable employee misconduct defense, an employer must show an adequate work rule, effective communication of it, methods to discover violations, and effective enforcement.
Several standards require specific training records or certifications, for example lockout/tagout, powered industrial trucks, process safety management, and bloodborne pathogens.
OSHA Outreach (10 and 30 hour) cards do not satisfy the training requirement of any OSHA standard.

sections.heading: What do OSHA compliance officers look at for training?

blocks.text: OSHA compliance safety and health officers (CSHOs) test training in three ways: they review written programs and records, they observe work during the walkaround, and they interview employees about what they were taught. The procedures are in the [Field Operations Manual](https://www.osha.gov/enforcement/directives/cpl-02-00-164), OSHA Instruction CPL 02-00-164, issued April 14, 2020 and updated by chapter since (Chapter 6 in July 2025 and Chapter 10 in February 2026).

items: **Opening conference.** [FOM Chapter 3](https://www.osha.gov/fom/chapter-3) tells CSHOs to outline the scope of the inspection, including private employee interviews, physical inspection, and records review.

**Programs and records.** Chapter 3 states that other OSHA programs and records will be reviewed, "including hazard communication, lockout/tagout, emergency evacuation and personal protective equipment," and that many standard specific directives tell CSHOs to request certain records at the opening conference.

**Employee interviews.** Section 8(a)(2) of the OSH Act authorizes CSHOs to question any employee privately, and the FOM treats interference, including management attempting to be present, as an issue for legal action. CSHOs are told to check whether an employee's English comprehension allows an effective interview and to use an interpreter where needed.

**Observation.** [FOM Chapter 5](https://www.osha.gov/fom/chapter-5) tells CSHOs to identify control techniques including employee training and education, and, where a standard requires an emergency action plan, to determine whether there is a training program for affected employees.

sections.heading: Why does training evidence affect whether a citation sticks?

blocks.text: Training evidence matters because it bears on two elements OSHA must establish or rebut: whether the employer knew or could have known of the hazard, and whether a violation was an isolated act of employee misconduct. Missing training does not only produce a training citation; it can make other citations easier to sustain.

blocks.title: FOM Chapter 4, knowledge of hazardous condition
blocks.text: Among the examples of evidence that an employer could have known of a hazard through reasonable diligence, the FOM lists: "The employer failed to train and supervise employees about the particular hazard." Where an employer says a supervisor's own conduct was isolated misconduct, CSHOs determine the extent to which the supervisor was trained in the rule and supervised.

[FOM Chapter 4](https://www.osha.gov/fom/chapter-4) and Chapter 5 together explain why. Chapter 5 sets out the elements of the unpreventable employee or supervisory misconduct defense: a work rule adequate to prevent the violation, effective communication of the rule to employees, methods for discovering violations of work rules, and effective enforcement when violations are discovered. CSHOs are told to document whether those elements are present, including whether the work rule tracks the requirements of the standard. A training record is the employer's main proof of effective communication.

sections.heading: Which OSHA standards require training records or certifications?

blocks.text: Most OSHA standards require training without prescribing a record, but several specify what must be documented. Have these ready first, because a missing certification is a straightforward citation. The table uses requirements already verified on the [OSHA training requirements page](/regulations/osha-training-requirements) and the standard specific pages linked.

sections.heading: What should be in the training evidence pack?

blocks.text: Build one pack per site that a manager can hand over at the opening conference. This original checklist follows the FOM's records review and interview approach.

items: Written programs for each applicable standard (hazard communication, lockout/tagout, emergency action, respiratory protection, personal protective equipment), with the training section of each highlighted.
A roster of employees by job, showing which standard specific training each job requires and the current status for each person.
The certifications and records in the table above, sorted by employee and filterable by department so you can produce any person's file quickly.

Training materials in the languages your workforce uses, consistent with OSHA's 2010 Training Standards Policy Statement that training must be presented in a manner employees are capable of understanding.
Trainer qualifications, especially where the standard requires knowledge, training, and experience (for example powered industrial truck trainers and evaluators).
Work rules, disciplinary policy, and records of enforcement, since FOM Chapter 4 lists employer work rules and disciplinary policies among documents CSHOs may obtain.
OSHA 300 logs, 300A summaries, and 301 reports for the past three years. Under 29 CFR 1904.40(a), the FOM notes, these must be provided within four business hours of a request.

blocks.title: Outreach cards are not compliance training
blocks.text: OSHA publication 2254 states that the Outreach Training Program is voluntary, does not meet the training requirements for any OSHA standard, and is not a certification. Standard specific training must be provided by the employer.

sections.heading: How should employees be prepared for interviews?

blocks.text: Employees cannot be coached on answers and managers cannot sit in on private interviews, so the only real preparation is training that people understood and remember. Check this before an inspection by asking a sample of workers, in their own words, how they lock out the machine they run or what they do after a needlestick.

items: Confirm that refresher cycles are current; the [refresh cycle guide](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles) explains how to set them by standard.
Use practical assessments for tasks with defined evaluation requirements, such as the powered industrial truck performance evaluation.
Tell employees, factually, that they may be interviewed in private and that the FOM informs them of their protections under Section 11(c) of the OSH Act.

sections.heading: What happens if training is found deficient?

blocks.text: Training deficiencies can be cited under the specific standard, and they can support citations for the underlying hazard. OSHA's maximum penalties for violations assessed after January 15, 2026 are $16,550 per serious or other than serious violation and $165,514 per willful or repeated violation. Powered industrial trucks (1910.178), a standard with detailed training and certification rules, is seventh on OSHA's preliminary fiscal year 2026 list of most frequently cited standards.

Twenty nine states and territories run OSHA approved State Plans that must be at least as effective as federal OSHA and may use their own procedures. The general method for assembling and sample testing records is in [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry maps each OSHA standard's training elements to job roles, assessments, and retraining triggers, so a site can show which workers were trained, on what, and how understanding was verified. See [compliance programs](/programs/compliance) and [energy and resources](/industries/energy-resources).

faqs.q: Can OSHA inspect training without notice?
faqs.a: Yes. FOM Chapter 3 describes advance notice as a narrow exception to the statutory prohibition, allowed only with Area Director authorization in limited situations. Training records therefore need to be retrievable at any time, not assembled after an inspection is announced.

faqs.q: Does OSHA require a signed training sign-in sheet?
faqs.a: Not generally. Some standards prescribe content, such as the lockout/tagout certification with names and dates or the bloodborne pathogens record with trainer qualifications and attendee job titles. Where no format is prescribed, any reliable record that shows who was trained, on what, when, and by whom will help.

faqs.q: Are online courses acceptable for OSHA training?
faqs.a: They can form part of training, but several standards require more. Powered industrial truck training must combine formal instruction, practical training, and evaluation of performance in the workplace, and the bloodborne pathogens standard requires an opportunity for interactive questions and answers with a knowledgeable person.

faqs.q: What if an employee says in interview that they were never trained?
faqs.a: The CSHO will compare the statement with your records. A record showing the person attended, what was covered, and how understanding was checked carries weight, but if the employee clearly cannot describe the procedure, OSHA may question whether training was effective or delivered in a way they could understand.
